passage: Diary, Friday. Chandrika here. Debate finals today and Amandeep beat me by two points. I wanted to be furious, and I was for about ten minutes, then I remembered his last rebuttal. It was so clever that I actually wrote it down. We walk the same way home so we ended up together, arguing about the topic all over again and laughing. Tanvi teased, "Are you two friends now?" and for a second I nearly said "no, he's just competition." I didn't. I said, "He's good, and that's why I have to work harder." I think that's true. Next round I want to beat him. And I want him there, because he makes me better. 🙂

qa.q: By how many points did Amandeep beat Chandrika?
Why did Chandrika almost say Amandeep was "just competition" to Tanvi, and why not in the end?
qa.a: Chandrika feared looking soft in front of a teasing friend, but admired Amandeep's work and knew the friendship was real, so Chandrika told the truth.

qa.q: How can rivalry help both people, according to Chandrika?
qa.a: It pushes each to work harder, as Chandrika writes that Amandeep "makes me better", and the friendship does not need hiding to compete.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chandrika after that walk home?
qa.a: Probably as both a challenger and a friend. They argued and laughed together on the way, so he likely enjoys the contest too.

grounding: Two rivals compete fiercely yet admire each other; the protagonist acknowledges the friendship and uses the rivalry as a push.

passage:
Music teacher's note, annual day rehearsals

Harish and Sudha are competing for the one solo slot in the senior choir piece, and both are working harder than I have ever seen. On Tuesday Sudha hit the high line cleanly and Harish, without thinking, said, "That was lovely." Then he noticed the boys at the back smirking and added, "For a girl who can't keep time." Sudha's face fell.

After rehearsal I asked him about it. He looked at the floor and said, "They'll say I'm soft on her."

We talked about how rivals who admire each other often both get better, and that pretending not to care costs more than it saves. On Thursday I saw him walk over to Sudha before the run-through and say, "Tuesday, what I said after was rubbish. You're the one I'm trying to catch." She laughed and said, "Then catch up."

Both of them sang better that day. I still have not decided the solo.

qa.q: What did Harish first say when Sudha hit the high line?
Why did Harish add the unkind comment after praising Sudha?
qa.a: He was worried the boys at the back would think him soft, so fear of looking weak pushed him to hide his real admiration.

qa.q: What did Harish do on Thursday that helped?
qa.a: He went to Sudha, admitted his comment was rubbish, and said openly that she was the one he was trying to catch.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Harish says she is the one he is trying to catch?
qa.a: Sudha probably feels respected and relieved, and her joking reply suggests she enjoys the friendly rivalry. 😊

grounding: It shows two fierce rivals who admire each other, the pull to deny that friendship to avoid looking soft, and how open respect lets the rivalry push both.

passage:
Saturday

Science fair results are out and I came second. Charu came first. Again. Her water-filter model was genuinely brilliant, the way she layered the charcoal and sand, and I told her so at the stall. She told me my solar dryer was "annoyingly clever." We both laughed like idiots.

Then on the bus Kunal and Rishi started on me. "You're supposed to hate her, bro. You're going soft." I almost said, "Charu? She's just lucky." The words were right there. I felt my face go hot and I hated that I cared what they thought.

I didn't say it. I said, "She's my friend and she beat me fair. Next year I'm beating her." They groaned. Whatever.

Honestly, having Charu to chase is the best part. She makes me check every wire twice. I'm going to ask her if we can test our designs together before the district round, just the two of us arguing about it.

— Yogesh

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Kunal and Rishi teased Yogesh on the bus?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and annoyed, with a hot face, because their opinion mattered and the urge to deny the friendship with Charu was strong.

qa.q: Which choice worked on the bus, and why?
qa.a: Calling Charu a friend who won fairly worked, because it kept the friendship honest while still showing Yogesh wanted to beat her next time.

qa.q: How might Charu see Yogesh's plan to test their designs together?
qa.a: Charu would likely enjoy it, since she already joked warmly about the solar dryer and seems to like being pushed by a rival she respects.

grounding: It shows two fierce rivals who admire each other's work, the temptation to deny the friendship to avoid looking soft, and the choice to let the rivalry push both.
